chunks: What has been narrated from the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم: that he performed tawaf and came out of the mosque, then began with al-Safa and said:

And his statement is in the form of a command, and it implies obligation: that one should begin in action with what Allah, Exalted is He, began with. If it is said: his statement, "Begin with what Allah began with," implies that they should begin in speech with what Allah began with in speech, while the disagreement only occurred regarding beginning in action — we say: it is not permissible to interpret that as speech for two reasons. One of them is that when he says, "Begin with what Allah began with," and that is a general expression under which both speech and action enter, then it is not for us to specify it except with evidence. The second is that he عليه السلام began in action with al-Safa and said, "Begin with what Allah began with," so that required: begin in action with what Allah began with in speech. If it is said, according to the first line of argument, that his statement عليه السلام, "Begin with what Allah began with," prevents carrying his statement "Begin" upon generality — do you not see that if a speaker says, "Strike Zayd with what 'Amr struck him with," and 'Amr only struck him with a staff, it would not be permissible to carry his statement "Strike Zayd" upon generality in everything with which one strikes; rather, it would be necessary to restrict it to that with which he was struck — we say: between the two matters there is a difference, because it is not possible for him to strike him in different ways other than with the staff and still be striking with what 'Amr struck him with. For this reason the speech was particularized to exactly that with which 'Amr struck him. But the report is not like this, because it is possible that they begin in speech and action with what Allah, Exalted is He, began with in speech, and when we begin with it in action, we are truly beginning with what Allah, Exalted is He, began with. Thus the difference between the two matters becomes clear, and this also indicates the obligation of sequence.

key_terms.الْفِعْلُ: Action; the main legal dispute concerns beginning in action.
key_terms.الْقَوْلُ: Speech; discussed here as one possible scope of the command.
key_terms.الْوُجُوبَ: Obligation; the passage argues that the wording of the command necessitates obligatoriness.
key_terms.اِبْدَءُوا: A command meaning to begin; here it is treated as implying legal obligation.
key_terms.بِالصَّفَا: Al-Safa; the Prophet’s صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم beginning there is used as practical proof.
key_terms.لَفْظَ عُمُومٍ: A general expression; one that includes more than one category unless restricted by evidence.
key_terms.وُجُوبِ التَّرْتِيبِ: The obligation of sequence; the legal conclusion derived from the report.

ai.seo_question: Does the hadith "Begin with what Allah began with" prove that sequence is obligatory in wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This passage argues that the prophetic command, "Begin with what Allah began with," is a legal command indicating obligation, not mere recommendation. It is used to establish the necessity of sequence in ritual acts, especially where Allah’s wording and the Prophet’s صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم practice together show that order in action must follow the divine order in speech.
